title: React Native — Native Layer, Platform & Shipping

topics.title: Native modules — when do you need one, and how do you write one?
topics.html:
• When: the platform API you need is not exposed to JS (a specific sensor, a payment SDK, a Bluetooth device), you must reuse an existing native SDK, or you need work that is too heavy for the JS thread.
  • Two kinds: a native module (functions you call — "get the battery level") and a native component (a real view you render — a map, a video player, a camera preview).
  • Autolinking means installing an npm package is usually enough; you rarely edit native project files by hand any more. On iOS you still run pod install.
Old (Bridge)New (TurboModule)
Declared byNative code, discovered at runtimeA TypeScript spec file, checked at build time
LoadedAll modules at app startupLazily, on first use
CallsAlways async, JSON onlyDirect through JSI, can be synchronous
Type safetyNone — runtime crashCodegen generates the glue, mismatch = build error
// Android side, old style — still useful to be able to read
public class DeviceModule extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule {
  @Override public String getName() { return "DeviceInfo"; }

  @ReactMethod
  public void getDeviceName(Promise promise) {
    promise.resolve(Build.MODEL);            // resolves the JS promise
  }
}

// JS side
import { NativeModules } from "react-native";
const name = await NativeModules.DeviceInfo.getDeviceName();
  • Sending events to JS: the native side emits through an event emitter and JS subscribes with NativeEventEmitter. Always remove the subscription on unmount.
  • Data crossing the boundary is limited to simple types — numbers, strings, booleans, arrays, plain maps. No functions, no class instances.
  • If you write one for production, remember it must exist twice — iOS and Android — plus the JS wrapper and the types.
💬 Say it like this

I reach for a native module when the capability simply is not available from JavaScript, or when an SDK we must use only ships native code. Most of the time autolinking means I just install a package, but I have had to write wrappers myself.

In the New Architecture the flow is nicer: I describe the module as a TypeScript spec, Codegen generates the C++ and platform glue, and the module is loaded lazily on first use instead of at startup. So a wrong argument type becomes a build error rather than a crash for a user.

Do you need to know Swift and Kotlin?
Not fluently, but a senior RN developer should be able to read them, patch a module, and debug a native crash stack trace. Say that honestly — pretending otherwise fails fast.
What is a "patch" workflow when a library is broken?
patch-package (or a pnpm patch) to fix it locally and commit the patch, while opening a PR upstream. Forking is the fallback for anything larger.

topics.title: iOS vs Android — the differences you have to design for.
topics.html:
AreaiOSAndroid
Back navigationSwipe from the left edge, back button in the headerHardware/gesture back — must be handled with BackHandler
ShadowsshadowColor / Offset / Opacity / Radiuselevation (also controls stacking)
Press feedbackOpacity / highlightRipple (android_ripple)
Safe areasNotch, home indicatorStatus bar, gesture bar, punch-hole cameras, huge variety
KeyboardKeyboardAvoidingView behavior="padding"windowSoftInputMode in the manifest
PermissionsAsked once; a "no" means Settings is the only way backRuntime prompts, plus "don't ask again"
Deep linksURL scheme + Universal Links (apple-app-site-association)Intent filters + App Links (assetlinks.json)
PushAPNs, user must accept the promptFCM, notification channels, runtime permission since Android 13
ReleaseApp Store review, TestFlightPlay Console tracks, staged rollout
  • In code: Platform.OS, Platform.select({ ios, android }), Platform.Version, or separate .ios.tsx / .android.tsx files that you import without the suffix.
  • Prefer one component with platform-specific styles over two whole components — until the behaviour genuinely differs, then split the file.
  • Android fragmentation is the real cost: many OS versions, many screen sizes, aggressive battery managers that kill background work, and vendor-specific bugs.
💬 Say it like this

The API is shared but the platforms are not. The ones that hit me in every project are the Android back button, which has no iOS equivalent, shadows being two different APIs, safe areas, and the keyboard, which is handled in JS on iOS and in the Android manifest.

My approach is to keep one component and branch only the styles with Platform.select, and split into platform files only when the behaviour is genuinely different. And I always test on a real low-end Android device, because that is where the differences and the performance problems both appear.

How do you keep platform branching from spreading everywhere?
Push it into the design-system layer — a Button or Card that knows about ripple and elevation — so screens stay platform-neutral.
What breaks most often on Android specifically?
Shadows and z-order, keyboard behaviour, background work being killed by the OS, and performance on low-end devices.

topics.title: Storage and offline — where does data live on the device?
topics.html:
OptionUse it forNotes
AsyncStorageSmall key/value data: settings, flags, cached JSONAsync, not encrypted, and has a size limit on Android by default
MMKVThe same, but fastSynchronous through JSI — no await. The common modern replacement.
SQLite / WatermelonDB / RealmReal relational or large offline dataQueries, migrations, proper offline-first apps
Keychain / KeystoreTokens, passwords, anything secretreact-native-keychain or expo-secure-store. Hardware-backed.
File systemDownloads, images, documentsRemember to clean up — users notice app storage size
  • Never put an auth token in AsyncStorage. It is plain text on disk. Secure storage exists for exactly this.
  • Offline-first pattern: React Query (or RTK Query) with a persisted cache, NetInfo to detect connectivity, optimistic updates for writes, and a queue of pending mutations replayed when the connection returns.
  • Then answer the hard part before they ask it: conflict resolution. Usually last-write-wins with a server timestamp, or a version field and a merge rule per entity.
  • Cache needs a policy: what is stale, what expires, and what must be re-fetched on app resume. "Cache everything forever" becomes a support ticket.
💬 Say it like this

For small key/value data I use MMKV, or AsyncStorage in older projects — but never for tokens, because it is unencrypted. Secrets go into the Keychain on iOS and the Keystore on Android through a secure storage library. For anything relational or genuinely offline-first I use SQLite.

For offline I persist the React Query cache so the app opens with data instead of a spinner, use NetInfo to know the state, and queue mutations to replay when the network comes back. The part people forget is conflict resolution — I decide up front whether the server timestamp wins or we merge per field.

MMKV vs AsyncStorage in one line?
MMKV is synchronous and much faster because it goes through JSI; AsyncStorage is promise-based and slower. Both are unencrypted by default, though MMKV supports encryption.
How do you version stored data?
Keep a schema version key, and write migration functions that run at startup. Without it, an app update on top of old cached shapes crashes on the user's phone and you cannot reproduce it.

topics.title: Push notifications, deep links and permissions.
topics.html:
Push, in the order it actually happens:

  • Ask the user for permission (iOS always; Android since 13 also needs a runtime permission).
  • Get a device token — APNs on iOS, FCM on Android — and send it to your backend with the user id.
  • The backend sends to APNs/FCM, not directly to the phone.
  • Handle three states in the app: foreground (show your own in-app UI), background (the OS shows it; you react to the tap), killed (the app launches from the notification — read the initial notification on startup).
  • Tokens rotate. Refresh and re-register, and remove tokens on logout or you send another user's notifications to the wrong person.
  • Libraries: expo-notifications, notifee, or React Native Firebase.

Deep links:

  • myapp://order/42 — a custom scheme, simple but any app can claim it.
  • Universal Links (iOS) and App Links (Android) use a real https URL verified by a file hosted on your domain. This is what you want for links sent by email or SMS, because they work even if the app is not installed.
  • In React Navigation you map URLs to screens with a linking config, and handle both "app was already open" and "app launched from the link".
  • Always validate the link. A deep link is untrusted input — never let it trigger a destructive action or skip an auth check.

Permissions:

  • Ask at the moment of use, with context — not a wall of prompts at first launch. Conversion is much higher and reviewers check this.
  • Handle every result: granted, denied, blocked / "never ask again", and restricted. For blocked, show an explanation and a button that opens system Settings.
  • Every permission needs a purpose string on iOS (Info.plist) and an entry in AndroidManifest.xml. A missing iOS purpose string is an instant App Store rejection.
💬 Say it like this

For push, the flow is: ask permission, get the APNs or FCM token, send it to our backend, and then handle the three app states — foreground, background, and launched from the notification when the app was killed. The detail people miss is token lifecycle: tokens rotate, and you must clear them on logout.

For deep links I prefer Universal Links and App Links over a custom scheme, because they are real https URLs verified by a file on our domain, so they work from email and cannot be hijacked by another app. And I treat the link as untrusted input — it can land the user on any screen, including while logged out.

For permissions the rule is simple: ask at the point of use with an explanation, and always handle the "blocked forever" case by sending the user to Settings.

How do you test a deep link?
npx uri-scheme open, or xcrun simctl openurl on iOS and adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "..." on Android.
What is a silent / data-only push?
A notification with no UI that wakes the app to sync data. iOS throttles them heavily and Android battery optimisation may drop them — never rely on them for correctness.

topics.title: How do you test a React Native app?
topics.html:
• Unit — Jest with the React Native preset. Pure logic, reducers, hooks, formatters. Fast and where most of your tests should be.
  • Component — @testing-library/react-native. Same philosophy as the web: query by what the user sees — getByText, getByRole, getByLabelText — and use testID only when there is nothing user-visible to target.
  • E2E — Detox (runs on a real simulator/emulator, synchronises with the app so it waits instead of sleeping) or Maestro (simple YAML flows, much easier to write and maintain). Maestro has become the popular choice for smoke tests.
  • Native modules must be mocked in Jest — they do not exist in Node. Most libraries ship a mock; otherwise jest.mock("react-native-xyz") in a setup file.
  • Snapshot tests: use sparingly. A huge snapshot gets approved blindly and tests nothing.
  • CI: Android builds anywhere, iOS builds need a macOS runner. That constraint shapes the whole pipeline — EAS Build, Bitrise, Codemagic or GitHub Actions with macOS.
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react-native";

test("submits the form", async () => {
  const onSubmit = jest.fn();
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);

  fireEvent.changeText(screen.getByLabelText("Email"), "a@b.com");
  fireEvent.press(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Log in" }));

  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: "a@b.com" });
});
💬 Say it like this

The pyramid is the same as on the web. Most of the value is in unit tests of logic, then component tests with Testing Library where I query the way a user would see the screen rather than by implementation details.

For end-to-end I use Detox or Maestro on a small set of critical flows — login, checkout — because mobile E2E is slow and flaky if you try to cover everything. The React Native specific part is that native modules have to be mocked in Jest, and that iOS builds need a macOS machine in CI, which is usually the thing that shapes the pipeline.

Why is mobile E2E flaky?
Animations, network timing and emulator startup. Detox reduces it by waiting for the app to be idle instead of using sleeps; beyond that, keep the suite small and run it on a fixed device image.
How do you test accessibility?
Use accessibilityLabel, accessibilityRole and accessibilityState, query by role in tests, and check with VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android. Labels also make your tests more stable than testIDs.

topics.title: Shipping — builds, over-the-air updates, and what you can and cannot hot-fix.
topics.html:
• The rule that matters: a change to JavaScript only can go out over the air. Anything touching native code — a new library with native parts, a permission, an RN upgrade, app icon or name — requires a new store build.
  • OTA tools: EAS Update (Expo) is the standard today; Microsoft's App Center CodePush was retired, and older projects moved to EAS or a self-hosted alternative.
  • OTA is not a free pass. Stores allow JS updates that do not change the app's purpose. Also ship updates gradually and keep a rollback ready — an OTA update can break every device at once.
  • Versioning: iOS has a version and a build number; Android has versionName and versionCode, and the code must always increase. Keep them in sync with your release process.
  • Distribution: TestFlight for iOS testers, Play Console internal/closed/open tracks for Android, staged rollout so a bad release reaches 5% and not 100%.
  • Crash reporting is mandatory: Sentry or Crashlytics with Hermes source maps uploaded per release, otherwise stack traces are unreadable bytecode.
  • Feature flags are how you turn a broken feature off without waiting for review. On mobile you cannot redeploy in five minutes, so flags do the job a deploy does on the web.
  • Upgrading RN: the React Native Upgrade Helper shows the exact diff of native files between versions; expo prebuild regenerates them for you. Budget real time for it — dependencies are the hard part, not the RN code.
💬 Say it like this

The mental model is: JavaScript changes can go out over the air with EAS Update, native changes need a new store build. So a broken text or a wrong API URL I can fix the same day, but adding a library with native code means a full release and review.

Because I cannot redeploy instantly like on the web, I lean on two things: staged rollouts, so a bad build only reaches a small percentage, and feature flags, so a broken feature can be switched off remotely. And every release uploads Hermes source maps to Sentry, otherwise the crash reports are useless.

What is the risk of OTA updates?
You can brick every install at once, and the JS bundle can get out of sync with the native code it expects. Always pin an update to a runtime/native version and roll out gradually.
How do you reduce app size?
Hermes, R8/Proguard, Android App Bundle, WebP assets, removing unused native SDKs, and checking what each dependency adds. App size measurably affects install conversion.

topics.title: Mobile security — what is different from the web?
topics.html:
• The bundle is readable. An APK is a zip; anyone can extract the JS bundle and read every string in it. So there are no secrets in the app — API keys, signing secrets and private endpoints belong on your backend.
  • Token storage: Keychain (iOS) / Keystore (Android) via a secure storage library. Never AsyncStorage. Prefer short-lived access tokens with refresh, and clear everything on logout.
  • Transport: HTTPS only, plus App Transport Security on iOS and a network security config on Android. Certificate pinning for high-value apps like banking — with a plan for rotating the pin, or you will brick the app when the certificate changes.
  • Deep links are untrusted input. Validate the target and never let a link perform an action without an auth check.
  • WebViews are the biggest hole: only load URLs you control, keep file access off, be careful with injectedJavaScript and postMessage, and never pass tokens into a WebView you do not own.
  • Rooted / jailbroken devices and repackaging — detection is possible but not a guarantee. Obfuscation raises the cost; it does not make anything safe.
  • Logs and screenshots: strip logs in release, and consider blocking screenshots or blurring the app switcher preview on sensitive screens.
  • Biometrics gate access locally — they are a convenience layer over a real token, not an authentication mechanism on their own.
  • OWASP Mobile Top 10 is the right thing to name here, the mobile counterpart to the OWASP web list in section 18.
💬 Say it like this

The biggest difference is that the attacker has the app. An APK is just a zip file, so the JavaScript bundle and every string in it can be read. That means no secrets ship in the app — anything sensitive lives behind our backend.

After that, the practical list is: tokens in the Keychain or Keystore rather than AsyncStorage, HTTPS everywhere with pinning if the data justifies it, deep links treated as untrusted input, and extreme care with WebViews, which are where most mobile vulnerabilities actually come from. I also strip logs in release builds and hide sensitive screens in the app switcher.

Is code obfuscation worth it?
It raises the effort for a casual attacker and is sometimes a compliance requirement, but it is not a security control. Design as if the bundle is public.
How do you handle a leaked API key?
Rotate it server-side immediately — you cannot recall an installed app. Then move the call behind your backend so the key never ships again. This is exactly why keys do not belong in the client.
